headlines.title: Who is Elizabeth Holmes and what did she do?
headlines.description: Elizabeth Holmes continues to be a pop culture fascination and cautionary tale of hubris among tech start-up founders. The former CEO of the health technology company is the subject of the new documentary, “You Can See Everything,” which hits theaters on Oct. 16. The trailer for the film went viral in September for its eerie interactions between Holmes and comedian Nathan Fielder as well as its depiction of Holmes’ family life with partner Billy Evans and their two young children. The film is just the latest project involving the saga of Holmes, which has previously spawned an HBO documentary and a scripted Hulu series. Here’s what to know about her story and the new film. Movies Sep 7 Crime and Courts Sep 24 Who is Elizabeth Holmes? Holmes dropped out of Stanford University at 19 years old in 2003 to start Theranos, a Silicon Valley company that promised to revolutionize healthcare. The company’s stated goal was to use technology to run hundreds of blood tests using only a simple pinprick of blood in a proprietary machine Theranos called the Edison. Holmes raised nearly $1 billion from several prominent investors, including Oracle founder Larry Ellison, media mogul Rupert Murdoch, and heirs of the Walton family that owns Walmart. By 2014, Theranos was valued at $9 billion. She became a darling of Silicon Valley, appearing on a 2014 cover of Forbes that billed her as the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire due to her 50% stake in Theranos. In 2015, she was named one of Time Magazine’s 100 most influential people. The company’s image began to unravel after a series of investigative articles by The Wall Street Journal in 2015 raised serious questions about whether the Theranos technology worked. The saga was also detailed in the 2018 book “Bad Blood” by WSJ journalist John Carreyrou. Theranos was using existing commercially available blood-analysis technology and repurposing it to run its blood tests, according to The Wall Street Journal. A former Theranos lab associate who became a whistleblower testified at Holmes’ trial that the Edison machines routinely failed quality control tests and that their results were about as accurate as “flipping a coin,” according to CNBC. An investigation into the company resulted in the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing civil fraud charges against Theranos, Holmes and former president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani. What did Elizabeth Holmes get convicted of? In January 2022, Holmes was convicted by a jury in a California court of four federal charges of wire fraud for misrepresenting to investors what the Theranos technology could do and how widely its Edison machines were being adopted. Prosecutors alleged that she duped investors into pouring money into a product she knew was faulty. Holmes denied the accusation during the trial. “At the time, you were not worried people would be given an inaccurate impression?” Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Leach asked her during the trial. “I was not,” Holmes said. Holmes was acquitted of charges of defrauding patients and one count of conspiracy. In May 2023, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila ordered her to pay $452 million in restitution to the victims of her crimes. Is Elizabeth Holmes still in prison? Yes, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022. Balwani was sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison and three years of probation after being convicted of 12 counts of fraud. Holmes, 42, has been serving her sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas, but she is expected to be let out of prison into a halfway house. She is scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims. Alan Eisenman, who invested about $1.2 million in Theranos, told NBC News on Sept. 24 that he was notified that she is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center in an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas. The Department of Justice is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails. Her scheduled release date is Feb. 22, 2030, after some reductions in her sentence. What makes the new movie different from previous projects? “You Can See Everything” is the latest film involving Holmes, and the most intimate. Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy for outstanding lead actress for her portrayal of Holmes in the 2022 scripted series “The Dropout” on Hulu. Holmes was also the subject of the 2019 HBO documentary “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.” In “You Can See Everything,” Holmes grants comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim extraordinary access to her life in the months leading up to when she entered prison. She had a son with partner Billy Evans in 2021 and then gave birth to a daughter in 2023, shortly before she began serving her prison sentence. The documentary trailer shows Holmes maintaining that she did nothing wrong and reveals that Fielder moved into her home while filming. “I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone,” she seemingly tells the comedian at one point. Evans also appears in the documentary and answers questions about his life with Holmes. There are also uncomfortable moments between Fielder and Holmes, including one in which he muses about whether he can trust her. “That’s because I don’t have anything to hide,” she tells him. This story first appeared on TODAY.com. More from TODAY: Hilary Swank, 52, Addresses Backlash Over Having a Baby Later in Life Baby Name Consultant Shares 1 Classic Baby Girl Name Nobody is Using — But Should What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis

headlines.title: Driver says he was asleep when Tesla crashed into CHP patrol car on I-80
headlines.description: Two California Highway Patrol officers are recovering after a Tesla hit one of their parked patrol cars on Interstate 80 in Fairfield earlier this week. CHP posted video online showing the crash, which happened Tuesday night west of Air Base Parkway. The officers were responding to a deadly crash when the Tesla drove through the crash site and hit the parked patrol car. The driver claimed he was asleep while using driver-assistance technology. It is unknown whether the Tesla’s Full Self-Driving feature was active at the time of the collision.

headlines.title: PG&E says power could be restored early for thousands in Bay Area
headlines.description: Thousands of people in the Bay Area are entering their second day without power, but the outage could end earlier than originally planned. PG&E has indicated that people in parts of the East Bay could have power restored around 4 p.m. Friday instead of around 2 p.m. Saturday as originally planned. Customers in the North Bay could have power restored around 7 p.m. Friday. PG&E’s outage website shows areas without power due to high fire risk, including parts of Contra Costa, Alameda, Sonoma and Napa counties. The utility shut off power to nearly 80,000 customers statewide, including around 6,200 in the East Bay, in what PG&E says is the largest Public Safety Power Shutoff since 2020. PG&E said it shut off the power to prevent power lines from sparking a wildfire amid hot, dry conditions that were expected to be windy. Some people without power have questioned PG&E’s decision because it hasn’t been windy in some locations. NBC Bay Area’s Bob Redell has the full report in the video above. East Bay 11 hours ago PG&E Oct 15 Bay Area Oct 14 PG&E Oct 13 PG&E warns Bay Area customers of possible shutoffs amid high winds, dry conditions

headlines.title: CTE study on NFL players raises questions about California's youth concussion protocol
headlines.description: There is renewed concern about whether enough is being done to prevent youth sports concussions following a major study that found at least a quarter of NFL players are expected to develop a degenerative brain disease. “What’s happening when these individuals are younger? How many little hits are they getting that leads to them having CTE,” asked Dr. Nirav Pandya, a pediatric orthopedic surgeon with UCSF Benioff who specializes in sports medicine for young athletes. “And what can we do at that younger age group to prevent these athletes from getting that?” Concussions in general affect around two million teenagers and children in the U.S. every year, according to the National Center for Health Statistics. Boys tackle football has the highest rate of concussions, according to the CDC, and girls soccer is number two. Girls have a higher change of sports-related concussions than boys, the agency said, in part because girls may report more and health care professionals like athletic trainers are less likely to be at girls’ practices and games to identify injuries. California’s student athlete concussion protocol In California, school coaches are required to take an online training course on concussions. If they suspect a concussion, they must remove the student athlete from the game or practice for at least that day until cleared by a licensed health care provider. If a concussion is confirmed, the student must complete a gradual return-to-play protocol lasting at least seven days. California’s student athlete concussion protocol. “I think the tough thing with all of this is that you are basing it on a kid reporting symptoms and someone identifying them,” said Dr. Pandya. He said he recently had a patient whose concussions went undiagnosed for over a year. “He had horrible headaches, had problems learning for over a year and had multiple concussions and hadn’t gotten treatment,” Dr. Pandya said. “A concussion, there’s no MRI; no blood test for it.” Reporter Candice Nguyen (left) and Dr. Nirav Pandya (right). Ben Nguyen’s concussion story Earlier this year, Ben Nguyen, a senior at Archbishop Mitty High School in San Jose, California, says he suffered a serious concussion during a wrestling match. “I felt incredibly nauseous,” he recalled. Nguyen shared cell phone video of the moment he got concussed. It shows his opponent go in for a takedown when Nguyen responds by trying to flip the other student over his own body. Image from video shared by Ben Nguyen. “His should and neck were kind of in my chin area,” he said. “The impact kind of went straight to my head.” The impact wasn’t obvious, but the symptoms afterward were. “I couldn’t think as fast anymore…I was like throwing up in the bus ride. I was throwing up right after my match as well,” Nguyen said. Nguyen said he felt a little nervous about telling his coach and athletic trainer, who’s a sports health care professional on the team. Ben Nguyen, Archbishop Mitty High School wrestler. “The impact looked so subtle. I was kind of scared of them being like, ‘Oh, there’s nothing, you can go back,’” Nguyen said. He said that didn’t happen and his school took his injury seriously. However, he admits, it’s easy for students to get around the concussion protocol if they want to. “I have a friend in football who had all the hallmark symptoms of concussions, he just lied on the survey to get back into practice,” he said. NBC Bay Area reached out to Archbishop Mitty High School. The school declined to participate in this story. The California Interscholastic Federation, which established the state’s student athlete concussion protocol, said it’s important for everyone involved to make sure the return-to-play process is followed. The solutions, the science, and the debate “If we can empower kids to understand that it’s okay to speak up. Number two, the system, athletic trainers, physical therapists, anyone who’s looking over these kids.Then, I think there are more drastic things that we talk about like, how can we decrease the number of chances or times that someone can get hit? Maybe that means delaying when kids start playing tackle football,” Dr. Pandya said. It’s some of those drastic suggestions that continue to be challenged. “My big concern is when we hear results about people who play the most elite level, that there’s a reaction of looking at, well, what do we do at the youth level? And these are very different games,” said David Camarillo who is Associate Professor of Bioengineering, (by courtesy) Mechanical Engineering and Neurosurgery at Stanford University. Camarillo has been studying concussions for the past 15 years testing thousands of helmets in his lab, CamLab, in Stanford. David Camarillo, Assoc. Professor of Bioengineering at Stanford University. The results he’s talking about come from a recent study published in the British Medical Journal showing at least a quarter of NFL players will likely develop a neurodegenerative disease like CTE. The NFL said it’s aware of the study, and it’s ensuring its community has access to expanding resources. Camarillo believes the science points to urgent action needed at the professional level. “Does it mean kids shouldn’t play sports? I don’t think we have enough information to say yes to that,” Camarillo said. When asked what’s the harm in taking preventative action in case certain youth sports are connected to developing CTE later in life, Camarillo said he believes taking action at an individual level is perfectly fair. “I think it’s a very different thing to make a law, to make public policy that affects everybody, that takes away a right to choose. That ought to have scientific evidence behind it,” he added. CamLab at Stanford University. Why isn’t there evidence? The British Medical Journal study relied on hundreds of NFL players donating their brains to science after they die. We don’t have that kind of data on our young athletes today. The Investigative Unit spoke to numerous doctors, researchers, and students about this issue over the past several weeks. All said the best solution right now is education, proper staffing for oversight, and schools fostering a culture where students feel encouraged to report concussion symptoms. “If it wasn’t for like my prior knowledge or like my friends or like me witnessing it first-hand, I probably would have lied to get back into wrestling,” Nguyen said. Candice Nguyen is the senior investigative reporter on this story. If you have a question about this story or a story tip, email her at candice.nguyen@nbcuni.com.

headlines.title: Lanes of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco to close this weekend
headlines.description: All southbound lanes and one northbound lane of Highway 101 at Hospital Curve in San Francisco will be closed this weekend for an ongoing construction project. The closure between Cesar Chavez Street and 17th Street will start at 11 p.m. Friday and continue until 6 a.m. Monday, according to Caltrans. Motorists should avoid the area and consider taking Interstate 280 as an alternate, Caltrans said. The closure will affect drivers heading out of San Francisco on the Central Freeway and those driving into San Francisco from the East Bay over the Bay Bridge, hoping through the city on highway 101. It will also affect those heading to Chase Center for the Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. This marks the third closure for the ongoing Hospital Curve repaving and rehabilitation project, which started last fall. The fourth and final closure – impacting the same lanes as this weekend’s closure – is scheduled for the weekend of Nov. 6-9, weather permitting, according to Caltrans.

headlines.title: L.A. County prosecutors weigh charges in Eric Swalwell case after sheriff's investigation
headlines.description: The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office sex crimes unit is weighing whether to bring charges in a case involving former Rep. Eric Swalwell, a spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday. The county sheriff’s victims’ unit investigated the case, which was then forwarded to prosecutors on Sept. 21, according to the spokesperson. Swalwell, a Democrat, resigned from Congress in April and dropped out of the California governor’s race after multiple sexual assault and misconduct allegations, which he denies. Former model and fashion software company owner Lonna Drewes held a news conference in April with her attorneys in Los Angeles, accusing Swalwell of drugging, sexually assaulting and choking her. Los Angeles authorities confirmed at the time that they had launched a criminal investigation into the allegations. An attorney for Swalwell said in an email Thursday that he is “innocent,” adding that “these allegations are false, and the facts will bear that out.” “The reported referral to the Los Angeles County District Attorney is a standard procedural step. It is not a charging decision. It is not a finding of wrongdoing. It changes nothing about the facts,” said the attorney, Sara Azari. “We welcome a fair, independent review, and we are confident it will vindicate him.” The FBI searched Swalwell’s Washington, D.C., home in August and seized an electronic device in connection with an investigation that was described as involving sexual misconduct allegations at the time, according to an official familiar with the matter. The same month, FBI agents executing a search warrant stopped Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and took his electronic devices. A copy of the search warrant obtained by NBC News detailed that investigators seized an iPhone and a MacBook Pro computer. The allegations first came to light in a San Francisco Chronicle article in which a former Swalwell aide said he had sexually assaulted her twice. A source familiar with the woman’s account confirmed to NBC News that the Chronicle’s reporting was accurate. The article was followed by a CNN report in which four women, including one whose story matched the Chronicle article, made sexual misconduct allegations against him. One of the three others, Ally Sammarco, said Swalwell sent her unsolicited photos of his penis; Sammarco later spoke to NBC News and confirmed the accuracy of her account in the CNN article. Swalwell denied the accusations published by the Chronicle and CNN in a video on social media on April 10, saying, “These allegations of sexual assault are flat false.” “They did not happen. They have never happened. And I will fight them with everything I have,” he said. Swalwell served in Congress for 13 years. A special election was held in June to fill the seat he vacated upon resignation; Democrat Aisha Wahab won the race to fill out the rest of his term. The election in November for a full two-year term will be a rematch between Wahab and fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez.
headlines.source: Andrew Blankstein and Raquel Coronell Uribe l NBC News

headlines.title: Neighbors frustrated after vandals target more San Jose schools
headlines.description: The list of South Bay schools hit by vandals continues to grow. Meyer Elementary School in San Jose is the latest campus targeted by vandals, who pulled and cut copper and electrical wire from underground cement boxes and panels. Windows were also smashed and the multipurpose room was ransacked. “Super sad because I went to school here and my kids went to school here,” said Dara Cano, who lives across the streety from Meyer Elementary School. Cano said her neighborhood is tired of seeing old school sites vandalized. Meyer was one of eight schools the Alum Rock Union Elementary School District closed last year. The district said six of those campuses remain vacant. Joseph George Middle School is one of the vacant campuses vandalized. The shuttered school was recently vandalized for a second time since closing, causing an estimated $200,000 in damage for the cash-strapped school district. The district is planning to discuss the vandalism at a special board meeting Thursday and frustrated neighbors are hopeful action will be taken to protect the schools. San Jose Oct 13 San Jose Oct 14 San Jose Oct 13

headlines.title: Los Gatos' ‘Fantasy of Lights' is walk-through only with fewer days this year
headlines.description: Big changes are in store this year for one of the South Bay’s biggest holiday attractions. Fantasy of Lights in Los Gatos will be cutting back the number of days it’s open significantly and switching from a mostly drive-through to an entirely walking format, the county confirmed. The county also noted that rising costs played a role in these changes. Fantasy of Lights is a county-run holiday light display that has been in existence since 1999. The event used to be exclusively a drive-through, where families would pack into their cars and drive through the 1.5-mile route at Vasona Lake County Park. But in recent years, organizers have added a couple of days when guests could walk the route. This year, the county confirms the event will be an only walk-through event. “We did not make this decision lightly,” said Audrey Ann Díaz, Acting Senior Communications Officer for Santa Clara County. “Like many beloved community traditions, Fantasy of Lights has faced rising operational costs over the years,” Díaz explained. She also noted that the walk-through events in the past have been “wildly successful,” complete with a drone show, live entertainment, and more food options. The event will also only run for four days this year from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m.: Saturday, Dec. 5 Sunday, Dec. 6 Saturday, Dec. 12 Sunday, Dec. 13 This new schedule is substantially shorter. In the past, the event has been for several walk-through-only days, followed by more than two weeks of drive-through days. It will be a noticeable change for families used to driving through the attraction, instead of paying for tickets per car, each person will need to purchase a ticket (tickets for those ages 13 and up are $25, tickets for youth ages 4-12 are $10, and tickets for children 3 and under are free). Tickets must be purchased in advance.

headlines.title: Oakland police tout drop in crime, but chief pushes for more progress
headlines.description: Oakland police on Thursday said crime is down across all major categories, but the chief acknowledged there’s still work to do. Chief James Beere said homicides this year are down more than 20% compared to the same period last year. Robberies and burglaries are down 26%. Beere said more needs to be done to address increases in larceny and robberies involving weapons. “I want to acknowledge something that’s very important. For those of us who have been victims of crime, these statistics may not reflect how you feel and how safe you feel,” Beere said. “We understand that and we take these concerns very seriously. At the same time, many of our residents have told us that they feel much safer.” Beere credited the decline in crime to collaboration between the community, city leadership and law enforcement partners. Beere acknowledged staffing remains a challenge. The police department currently has 601 officers. Beere pointed to a recent audit that found the department needs at least 877 officers to maintain its current level of service. Oakland 20 hours ago Oakland 24 hours ago

headlines.title: Trump administration sues California to block state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots
headlines.description: The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month’s midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. The lawsuit follows a letter sent earlier this week by a top Justice Department official who threatened potential legal action if California didn’t comply. The federal government didn’t specify where the 20,000 voters were concentrated, but the list was sent directly to Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan on Tuesday, his office confirmed in a statement. His office said the list contained names of voters throughout California, not just Los Angeles, even though Logan is the only county election official named as a defendant in the lawsuit. He doesn’t have jurisdiction over ballots outside Los Angeles County. In a statement Thursday, Logan said his office can’t withhold ballots or refuse to count them “based solely on unverified allegations.” Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and there are a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts that could determine which party has control of the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Expert says lawsuit could set stage for false election claims California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn’t provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state’s voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government initially alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada’s voter rolls, but the state determined that all the people flagged were, in fact, U.S. citizens. She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.” California’s elections are in “full compliance” with federal law, she added. David Becker, an election law expert who heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research, called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “fairly frivolous.” “If they were seeking to work in good faith to clean up the voter list that they believed had issues, they would have done this months ago in a much different fashion,” Becker said. “However, it does raise questions as to whether or not the sole purpose of this is to set the stage for false claims about elections.” List of alleged illegal voters delivered on a thumb drive Logan said his office received the thumb drive along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.” Becker said most election officials’ cybersecurity protocols would not allow them to comply with the Justice Department’s request as it was sent. “Election offices do not just stick thumb drives into their technology, for very good reason,” he said. The Justice Department’s lawsuit says the federal government sought to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and “California made no serious effort to do so.” “The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question,” the lawsuit says. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined.” Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government’s outreach had not been collaborative. She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them. In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands “an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.” Letters sent weeks before elections The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their immigration status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government’s requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration’s alleged number of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department. “What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong,” Bonta said. He also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election. “They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory,” he said. The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, defended the Justice Department’s move to take California to court. “This is not political or controversial,” he wrote in a post on X. “We will not allow California to dilute the votes of American citizens.” ___ Austin reported from Sacramento, Riddle from Los Angeles and Durkin Richer from Washington. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed. .
headlines.source: Alanna Durkin Richer | The Associated Press, Sophie Austin | The Associated Press and Safiyah Riddle | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. headlines.title: Bay Area company's air taxi in final stages of testing with FAA
headlines.description: A Bay Area company is testing new technology that could one day have people flying over the streets instead of driving on them. San Jose-based Archer Aviation has created an electric air taxi, and the company was out in Oakland Thursday performing test flights. “This beautiful aircraft is an air taxi that’s under development at the company,” Archer Aviation Chief Strategy Officer Eric Lentell said. “We’re going through kind of the final stages of testing with the FAA to be able to bring it to market.” The goal is to defeat traffic congestion in cities, while being competitive with Uber Black or Uber Premiere pricing. “Really focused on kind of 10- to 20-mile routes where it takes about 60 to 90 minutes in a car and we can do in about 10 minutes,” Lentell said. An air taxi seats four people, plus a pilot. The technology is similar to an electric car but in an aircraft. The company has focused on both conventional and vertical takeoffs and landings. “The big change, the big step change is distributed electric propulsion,” Lentell said. “With going all electric on an aircraft instead of a typical combustion engine, you can rethink the design of these aircraft.”
